newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast premier to discuss debt, trade in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast premier to discuss debt, trade in U.S..

text.p: Ivory Coast Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan visits the United States and Canada next week for talks on promoting trade and easing his West African country's debt burden.
Duncan, who left for Paris late on Thursday en route for North America, launches the U.S. leg of his trip on Monday.
Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, is trying to strengthen its economy by encouraging private investment and broadening its economic base beyond farm products.
Duncan, promoting his nation under the slogan Ivory Coast the Elephant of Africa, has already visited Europe and Asia to outline business opportunities.
But his country's foreign debt -- around $15 billion -- is likely to feature highly on the agenda.
Ivory Coast says that the commercial banks, grouped in the London Club and owed around $7 billion, are trying to drive too hard a bargain.
Ivory Coast was among Africa's top performing economies in 1995, notching up growth of seven percent and keeping inflation in single figures -- seven percent against a target of five percent.
But the government, arguing that in the past its exports have been at the mercy of unpredictable world prices, is seeking a new payment schedule.
Duncan, addressing the American Chamber of Commerce in Ivory Coast's main city Abidjan last week, highlighted the need for help with the foreign debt.

"Our desire is that the United States continues to support Ivory Coast on the important issues of the expected March 1997 rescheduling of the public foreign debt and the talks with the London Club on a concessionary settlement of the commercial debt," he said.
After a commodities-led boom following independence from France in 1960, Ivory Coast's economy slumped in the mid-1980s as world prices fell.
President Henri Konan Bedie, formally elected last October after taking over on the 1993 death of independence president Felix Houphouet-Boigny, is keen to build a broader economic base.

The government is looking to processing more Ivorian raw materials at home -- 50 percent of the cocoa output by the year 2000 from about 18 percent now -- and to expand its energy and minerals sector, which includes oil, gas, diamond and precious and other metals.
